title: Zwingli's sausages
hook: in Zurich, eating sausages in Lent starts a reformation

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's Small Catechism, a thin book for teaching at home, and its one question. Your line was what does this mean?

The presses at a Zurich print shop have been running hard. The printer, Christoph Froschauer, has a big job due, and his workers are worn out. It's Lent, the season before Easter, when the church of their day forbids meat. At a meal in the printer's house, the story goes, someone brings out sausages, cut up and shared around the table. A local priest is in the room: Huldrych Zwingli. Word gets out, the city council gets involved, and a plate of sausages turns into a public question about the whole church.

Here's the odd part. By the usual account, Zwingli didn't eat any. He sat at the table and let it happen. But when the eaters were accused, he stood up for them, in a sermon later printed as On the Choice and Freedom of Foods. His argument went to the Bible: where does scripture command this? He pointed to Paul, in the King James Bible: "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday." Fasting, Zwingli said, can be a good thing, and anyone who wants to fast in Lent should be free to. But it shouldn't be a law that binds every conscience under threat of punishment. That's the hinge: not a rule against fasting, but a question about who gets to make the rule. Once Zurich asked that about sausages, it asked it about everything else, until the city's church was reshaped around preaching from scripture. Paul has a second line that cuts both ways: "Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth." The eater shouldn't sneer. The faster shouldn't judge. Christians keep Lent in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep the Lenten fast together, as a discipline of the whole church. Some Protestant Christians fast by choice, or give something up. Underneath it all is Zwingli's honest question: why do we do this?
screen: `LET NO MAN JUDGE YOU IN MEAT.`

segments.voice: Think of one rule you keep without thinking: a religious habit, a family custom, the way things are always done at work. Ask Zwingli's question gently, why do we do this, and look for the reason; sometimes there's a good one, and sometimes it's just habit. If you pray, ask for wisdom about it; if you don't, hold the rule up to the light for a while.
Zwingli's sausages. A meal in Lent in a Zurich print shop that Zwingli defended, and a question about rules that reshaped a city's church.
Your line: why do we do this? One honest question reshaped a whole city's church. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep set fasts in Lent, such as abstaining from meat on certain days; some Protestant Christians fast or give something up by personal choice during Lent.
